title: Sharper than a sword
hook: the devotees' way is unique, sharper than a sword and finer than a hair (Anand 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, doubt, and your line, the word clears. Did a shabad or a song fill the room? Today, pauri fourteen, and a path that's very narrow indeed. Day three hundred ninety.

Watch a child walk along a curb like a balance beam. Arms out, one foot in front of the other, eyes fixed ahead, while everyone else just walks on the sidewalk. One wobble and she's off. It takes total attention, and it's strangely absorbing. Now imagine the curb gets thinner, sharp as a blade, fine as a single hair. And imagine somebody telling you that this, not the wide sidewalk, is the path of those who love God. That's the fourteenth pauri of Anand Sahib. Today: sharper than a sword.
screen: `WALKING A CURB, ARMS OUT.` → `ONE WOBBLE AND YOU'RE OFF.` → `NOW, THINNER THAN A HAIR.`

segments.voice: The pauri opens: bhagtaa kee chaal niraalee. The way of the devotees is unique, unlike any other. Niraalee means distinct, set apart, one of a kind. Then, in paraphrase: the way of the devotees is distinct; they walk a hard path. They give up greed, grasping, ego and craving, and they don't talk too much. Then the famous image, transliterated: khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee, et maarag jaanaa. Sharper than a double-edged sword, finer than a hair: that is the path they walk. Those who, by the Guru's grace, let go of self, their desire merges into the Lord. Says Nanak, the way of the devotees, age after age, is unique. Two details stand out. First, khanniahu, from khanda, the double-edged sword. Guru Amar Das was reaching for an everyday picture of sharpness. More than a century later, in 1699, a khanda would stir the amrit at the first Khalsa initiation, and today it stands at the center of the Sikh emblem, so Sikhs now hear this line with that blade in mind. Second, look at the list of what's given up. Greed, grasping, ego, craving. And then, almost funny in its plainness: talking too much. Not some great austerity. Just fewer words. That's the hard path. It isn't hard because it's exotic. It's hard because it's narrow. Every day, a hundred small chances to step off: a greedy thought, a proud word, one more thing to grab. The devotee's way is to stay on the line, again and again. And notice how the pauri ends: the ones who stay on the line are those who, by the Guru's grace, have let go of self, and whose desire merges into the Lord.
screen: `NIRAALEE: SET APART, UNIQUE.` · `GIVE UP GREED, EGO, CRAVING.` · `AND DON'T TALK TOO MUCH.` · `SHARPER THAN A KHANDA, FINER THAN A HAIR.` · then, large: `THE NARROW WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one narrow line carefully. If you can, stand up and find a line on the floor: a floorboard seam, the edge of a rug, a tile joint. Walk slowly along it, heel to toe, arms out if you need them, for a few steps. Notice the attention it takes. Notice how the mind goes quiet when it has one thing to do. Then sit and breathe. If you can't stand, trace a line slowly with one finger. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each careful step. The bell holds the time.
Sharper than a sword. Khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee: the devotees' way is sharper than a double-edged sword and finer than a hair, and walked by letting go of self.
Your line: the narrow way. Today, take the narrow way in one small thing: say fewer words in one conversation than you normally would. Day three hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and the khanda, the double-edged sword it names, is used to stir the amrit at the Khalsa initiation.

fork.setup: you want to walk the way of the devotees. according to pauri fourteen, what is that path like?
options: wide and comfortable, open to any pace.
sharper than a double-edged sword, finer than a hair.
fork.reveal: khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee: sharper than a khanda, finer than a hair. and walked by letting go of self, by the Guru's grace.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sharper than a double-edged sword, the opening of Anand's most famous image.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line saying faith is impossibly hard.
what it means: the devotees' way is narrow, sharper than a sword and finer than a hair, walked by letting go of greed, ego and too many words.
what a scholar hears: khanniahu is from khanda, the double-edged sword later used to prepare amrit, and vaalahu from vaal, hair: the pauri's two images measure the path from both sides.

notes: Pauri 14 paraphrased ('bhagtaa kee chaal niraalee; chaalaa niraalee bhagtaahaa keree bikham maarag chalnaa; lab lobh ahankaar taj trisnaa bahut naahee bolnaa; ... gur parsaadee jinee aap tajiaa har vaasnaa samaanee; kahai naanak chaal bhagtaa jugahu jug niraalee'). Confirm transliteration, Ang and pauri number.
Khanniahu glossed from khanda (double-edged sword). The khanda's use in amrit preparation dates from 1699, after Guru Amar Das; the trapdoor says 'later used'. Confirm.

Audit (2026-10-01): the teach implied Guru Amar Das's image pointed to the amrit khanda; it now says the khanda's amrit use came in 1699, more than a century later. Replaced stock phrases ('deep Sikh resonance', 'make this line sing'), the templated 'Have you ever' opening and the slogan ending.
